content: The studies conducted by Haroon et al. (1996) and Jerajani et al. (2013) were open trials, which inherently carried a high risk of bias due to the lack of blinding. Both studies also reported high attrition rates of 20% and 25%, respectively. In other studies, the processes of sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding were assessed as having an unclear risk of bias. Additionally, there was substantial heterogeneity across the studies (I² = 75%), with six different azole creams and varying allylamine treatment regimens being used. Jerajani et al. (2013) was specifically noted for its high risk of bias due to the absence of blinding and a high attrition rate. The remaining studies also had unclear risks of bias in sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding. The number of events in these studies was low, with wide confidence intervals (CIs) that included potential harm, no effect, and appreciable benefit. An optimal sample size of 15,414 participants was estimated to be necessary for more reliable results. The total number of participants across the studies was low, and the wide CIs further reduced the reliability of the findings. One study included only nine participants in total. When comparing azoles to benzylamines for the treatment of tinea cruris and tinea corporis, the quality of evidence was rated as very low due to significant limitations in study design, including high risks of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. For example, Ramam et al. (2003) was judged to have a high risk of bias due to a high attrition rate and industry funding of both interventions. Different azole formulations were assessed across studies, and substantial heterogeneity was observed, making it difficult to pool data. The sample sizes were small, with optimal sizes estimated to be around 5,500 participants, and the CIs were very wide, including both harm and benefit. For the comparison of azoles versus placebo in tinea cruris and tinea corporis, the evidence quality was also very low. Studies such as those by Miura et al. (1979) and Spiekermann & Young (1976) were judged to have high risks of bias due to high attrition rates and industry funding. Sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding were unclear across the studies. Substantial unexplained heterogeneity was present, and data were not pooled due to these inconsistencies. The sample sizes were small, and the CIs were wide, including null effects and appreciable harm. In the context of HIV-associated conditions, the quality of evidence for various treatments was consistently low or very low. For example, studies comparing acyclovir to placebo for herpes zoster in HIV-infected individuals lacked details on randomization and included non-HIV populations, leading to low-quality evidence. Similarly, comparisons of famciclovir versus acyclovir and brivudin versus acyclovir for herpes zoster were also rated as low quality due to incomplete randomization details and the inclusion of non-HIV populations. For scabies treatment, comparisons of topical permethrin versus oral ivermectin, as well as other regimens, were rated as very low quality. Issues included poor confirmation of diagnosis, unclear definitions of clinical cure, lack of blinding, and small sample sizes. For example, studies comparing oral ivermectin with benzyl benzoate or combined therapies in HIV-positive patients were retrospective, observational, and involved small populations, further reducing the reliability of the findings. In the management of oropharyngeal candidiasis associated with HIV, comparisons of fluconazole with other antifungal agents such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, clotrimazole, and nystatin were also rated as low or very low quality. Common issues included lack of blinding, unclear randomization methods, small sample sizes, and wide CIs that included null effects. For example, studies comparing fluconazole to itraconazole or clotrimazole had significant heterogeneity and imprecision, with total event numbers below 300. Overall, the evidence for the treatment of skin and oral conditions associated with HIV infection in children and adults was limited by small sample sizes, high risks of bias, and wide confidence intervals. Many studies lacked rigorous methodologies, including proper randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding, which significantly impacted the reliability of the findings.
